topics.title: Coursework
topics.summary: Marked work: if an instructor says no outside assistance is permitted, using generative AI is typically treated as an unauthorized aid under the Code; instructors are asked to state their rules in the syllabus. Separately, students may generally use AI as a learning aid (to summarize or test understanding) even when a course bans AI for assignments, and such study use usually need not be disclosed.

claims.text: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

claims.text: The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

topics.title: Privacy & sensitive data
topics.summary: Before sharing personal information or Level 2-4 university data with any AI tool, verify it has been assessed for that level; AI Kitchen tools are approved up to Level 3 (the Model Comparison Tool only to Level 2). Without the instructor's explicit permission, students may not upload course materials (slides, recordings, test questions, rubrics) to an AI tool not approved for that purpose. Instructors using unvetted third-party AI tools must let students opt out with a viable alternative, and a Privacy Impact Assessment is required when personal information is collected.

claims.text: The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

additionalTopics.title: Security & procurement
additionalTopics.summary: Before sharing personal information or Level 2–4 university data with any AI tool, users must verify that the tool has been assessed by the university as suitable for that classification level. Central AI Kitchen tools are approved up to Level 3 (Model Comparison Tool only up to Level 2). When instructors use unvetted third-party AI tools in courses, students must be provided a viable opt-out alternative, and a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) is required wherever personal information is collected.
additionalTopics.scope: Information Security AI guidelines and CTSI non-supported tool guidance; institutional data levels and course PIA requirements.

claims.text: University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.
